name: Siksika
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Siksika/Blackfoot is not in the catalog. Two title hits: Van Der Mark 2003 (MA thesis, already on file from the earlier pass) is squarely about word-level pitch accent and states it is primarily lexical, one accent per word, with an inconsistent preference for heavy syllables (§2.2.5 pp. 11-12); Both and. Best first-hand statement: Van Der Mark 2003 §2.2.5, corroborated by Stacy 2004, Elfner 2006, Frantz 1970, Uhlenbeck 1938 and the Van der Mark 2002 summary of Kaneko 1999 (heavy syllable takes accent; leftmost heavy if several; lexical when all light). Still unread and worth acquiring for a fuller rule: Kaneko 1999 (UBC MA), Frantz 1991/2009 Blackfoot Grammar (pp. 3, 34), Taylor 1969 (p. 25), Weber 2020 (UBC PhD). all access went through DOI/API/curl.

new_statements.quote: Blackfoot PA is primarily lexical. Blackfoot words typically contain one pitch accent; no words are accentless, while some words contain more than one PA. However, multiple PAs [are] uncommon, occurring in a few types of poly-morphemic words such as compounds or verb complexes. A PA can occur on either a long or short vowel. [...] Syllable weight appears to interact with PA in Blackfoot, though not consistently. Kaneko (1999) notes that PA tends to fall o[n] heavy syllables. While there are numerous exceptions to this generalization, it appears to be an active component of the Siksika grammar in that other phonological changes fall from this fact.
new_statements.citation: Van Der Mark, Sheena Chantal. 2003. The phonetics of Blackfoot pitch accent. MA thesis, University of Calgary. §2.2.5 'Pitch accent', p. 11.
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences

new_statements.rule_in_words: Blackfoot is a pitch-accent language: each word normally carries one lexically specified high-pitch accent (marked with an acute in Frantz's orthography) whose position is not predictable from syllable count or word edge; it may fall on a long or short vowel anywhere in the word. Tendencies reported but not rules: accent prefers heavy syllables (leftmost heavy in monomorphemic nouns, Kaneko 1999 via Van der Mark 2002:181), often sits near the left edge and avoids the right edge (Stacy 2004). Elfner 2006:14 sums up: 'accent placement in Blackfoot is virtually unpredictable, although some generalisations exist'. Frantz 1991:34, 65 (via Stacy) says the accent-assignment rules are 'poorly understood'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress in the modern accounts (culminative single PA; extra PAs in compounds are treated as multiple accents, not secondary). Uhlenbeck 1938:9-10 marks a 'secondary stress or stresses' with the grave in Southern Peigan, and says it is often impossible to decide which stress is strongest.
new_statements.exceptions: Multiple PAs in some compounds and verb complexes; contour (rising/falling) PAs on long vowels linked to one mora; weight tendency has 'numerous exceptions'. Stacy 2004:11-12, 75: ~10% of imperatives take a discourse-driven accent on the stem-final vowel; devoiced ('deficient') syllables and right-edge elements do not bear accent; some polymorphemic words surface with no accent or with adjacent accents. Uhlenbeck 1938:9 (Southern Peigan) reports 'wavering stress' and disyllables with equal stress on both syllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: elicited citation forms of nouns and verbs from five Siksika-dialect speakers (ch. 5, p. 35). Frantz 1991:3 (quoted in Stacy 2004:55) notes utterance-level declination, so a late accented syllable may be lower in absolute pitch than an earlier unaccented one but remains high relative to the following syllable.
new_statements.identity_note: siks1238 is the language-level code for Blackfoot/Blackfeet (Siksika, Kainai/Blood, Piikani/Peigan, Aamsskaapipikani/South Peigan dialects). The quoted statement (Van Der Mark 2003) describes the Siksika dialect specifically (five Siksika Nation speakers, Alberta); Kaneko 1999's weight generalisations come from Blood (Kainai) speakers; Uhlenbeck 1938's expiratory-stress description is Southern Peigan (Montana, 1910s data). Frantz 1991 covers Blackfoot generally. All sources treat the accent system as shared across dialects.

new_statements.reading: Blackfoot (Siksika) word prominence is a lexically specified pitch accent, culminative in the sense that every word carries at least one accent, with a weak weight attraction (heavy syllables preferred, many exceptions). No fixed positional stress rule. Corroborated first-hand by Stacy 2004 §2.3.4 pp. 11-12 ('Accent is mainly lexical in Blackfoot'; prominence avoids the right edge of the word; Taylor 1969:25 said any syllable can be stressed), by Elfner 2006 §2.3.3 p. 14 ('accent placement in Blackfoot is virtually unpredictable'), by Frantz 1970 ('word stress patterns appear to be a function of both vowel length and inherent stress of certain syllables'), and by Uhlenbeck 1938 §5 pp. 9-10 (one or more expiratory accents per word, position varies, 'wavering stress'). Van der Mark 2002:181 summarises Kaneko 1999's nominal rule: a single heavy syllable takes the accent, leftmost heavy if several, lexical if all light. Suggested coding: lexical/unpredictable accent (pitch-accent type), weight-sensitive tendency.

sources.citation: Van Der Mark, Sheena Chantal. 2003. The phonetics of Blackfoot pitch accent. MA thesis, University of Calgary. §2.2.5 'Pitch accent', p. 11.
sources.quote: Blackfoot PA is primarily lexical. Blackfoot words typically contain one pitch accent; no words are accentless, while some words contain more than one PA. However, multiple PAs [are] uncommon, occurring in a few types of poly-morphemic words such as compounds or verb complexes. A PA can occur on either a long or short vowel. [...] Syllable weight appears to interact with PA in Blackfoot, though not consistently. Kaneko (1999) notes that PA tends to fall o[n] heavy syllables. While there are numerous exceptions to this generalization, it appears to be an active component of the Siksika grammar in that other phonological changes fall from this fact.
sources.note: §2.2.5 p. 11: Blackfoot pitch accent (PA) is primarily lexical; one PA per word typically, no accentless words, occasional multiple PAs in compounds/verb complexes; PA on long or short vowels; rising/falling contour PAs on long vowels; weight interacts inconsistently (Kaneko: PA tends to fall on heavy syllables, many exceptions). Instrumental chapters 6-8 show F0 is the main correlate, with intensity and duration also higher on accented vowels; consultants = five Siksika-dialect speakers (p. 35).

sources.citation: Windsor, Joseph W. (2017). Predicting prosodic structure by morphosyntactic category: A case study of Blackfoot. Glossa: a journal of general linguistics 2(1): 10, pp. 1-17.
sources.quote: Blackfoot orthographic convention (Frantz 1978) is to write pitch accented vowels with accents. Long vowels and consonants, which are contrastive (Frantz 1978; 2009; Frantz & Russell 1995; Elfner 2006), are written as double letters. [p. 1 fn. 1] ... it is possible to analyze the plural morpheme -iksi as being a sequence of syllables, possibly a metrical foot. However, because this suffix does not appear to contribute stress to any of the tokens analyzed, there is no reason to assume a metrical foot is the correct analysis of this structure. [p. 11]
sources.note: Paper is about prosodic constituency (syllable vs prosodic word vs phonological phrase), diagnosed by vowel coalescence and right-edge aspiration, and its mapping to morphosyntactic categories. It contains no statement of where word-level pitch accent/stress falls; the only accent remarks are the orthographic footnote and the aside that the plural suffix -iksi bears no stress in the tokens analysed.

sources.citation: Frantz, Donald G. 1970. Toward a generative grammar of Blackfoot (with particular attention to selected stem formation processes). PhD dissertation, University of Alberta (SIL 1971 reprint).
sources.note: §0.3: underlining marks 'stress (prominence) of the vowel (as marked primarily by pitch)'; acute accent marks 'inherent stress' in underlying forms; 'Word stress patterns appear to be a function of both vowel length and inherent stress of certain syllables, although analysis of this system is still incomplete'; rules sensitive to verb vs noun status (nitomitáama vs nitomitaami).

sources.citation: Elfner, Emily Jane. 2006. The mora in Blackfoot. MA thesis, University of Calgary.
sources.note: §2.3.3 p. 14: 'Blackfoot is a pitch accent language (Frantz 1978, 1991; Van Der Mark 2003; Stacy 2004). Unlike stress, accent placement in Blackfoot is virtually unpredictable, although some generalisations exist (Frantz 1978, 1991).' Prominence otherwise left for future research.

sources.citation: Stacy, Elizabeth. 2004. Phonological aspects of Blackfoot prominence. MA thesis, University of Calgary.
sources.note: §2.3.4 pp. 11-12: 'Accent is mainly lexical in Blackfoot, although it may be discourse driven to some degree' (imperatives ~10% final-vowel accent); 'To date in the Blackfoot literature, there are no noted restrictions on where PA can fall... Taylor (1969:25) states that any syllable can be stressed'; deficient (devoiced) syllables and right-edge elements do not bear accent. §4.3-4.4 pp. 72-76: culminativity holds in many words but is 'very frequently contravened' (multiple PAs, accentless words, adjacent accents); PA often near the left edge. pp. 55-56 quote Frantz 1991:3, 34, 65 second-hand.

sources.citation: Van der Mark, Sheena. 2002. The acoustic correlates of Blackfoot prominence. Calgary Working Papers in Linguistics 24: 169-216.
sources.note: §3.3 p. 181 summarises Kaneko 1999: mixed lexical and fixed system; in monomorphemic nouns a heavy syllable (long vowel or coda) carries prominence, leftmost heavy if several, lexically specified if no heavy syllable; compounds keep the leftmost accent (moved to the juncture if final), default final syllable if neither member is accented.

sources.citation: Uhlenbeck, C. C. 1938. A concise Blackfoot grammar, based on material from the Southern Peigans. Amsterdam: Noord-Hollandsche Uitgevers-Maatschappij. 235 pp.
sources.note: Ch. I §5 'Stress' pp. 9-10: 'In Blackfoot words, on one syllable, or very often even on two or more syllables, a strong expiratory accent may be observed'; acute = strongest accent, grave = secondary stress; often impossible to decide which is stronger; disyllables with equal stress on both syllables (nokós/nókos), demonstratives with shifting accent (omá : óma); no placement rule given ('numerous cases of wavering stress'). Southern Peigan (Montana) material.
